problems.issue: The defining skeletal phenotype is substantially underreported: platyspondyly 10%, kyphoscoliosis 12%, flared metaphyses 12%, and hypoplastic iliac bodies 20%, versus 91–100% in R1-train. Despite possible ascertainment differences, this loses the recognizable spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia pattern.

Joint laxity is poorly represented: finger joint hypermobility is reported in only 2%, versus 55% in R1-train, with no prominent broader joint-hypermobility term shown. Soft, doughy skin is likewise reported in only 2%, suppressing the characteristic connective-tissue phenotype.

Examples contain distracting, atypical findings such as elevated fecal sodium, increased IgG, delayed CNS myelination, and fatty replacement of skeletal muscle. Example 1 lacks a recognizable defining phenotype, while example 3 emphasizes ocular, biochemical, and endocrine findings over skeletal dysplasia and laxity.
Atrial septal defect is reported in 29% and outranks nearly every defining skeletal feature. Although cardiac abnormalities can occur, this prominence needs supporting evidence.

summary: Sex balance and young presentation are plausible, but hallmark underreporting and atypical findings would teach a misleading disease profile. No literature panel is provided to assess true-rate calibration directly.
